Linear algebra

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Algebra
OurBigBook.com Words: 73k Articles: 1k
Linear algebra studies vector spaces and linear maps: operations that preserve vector addition and scalar multiplication. For a linear map T, the defining rule is T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v), where u,v are vectors and a,b belong to the underlying field. The vectors might be arrows, lists of measurements, or polynomials. What matters is that their linear combinations make sense and that the same rule governs their transformation.
A concrete linear map is T(x,y)=(x+y,x−y). Its two outputs record a sum and a difference. Since T(1,0)=(1,1) and T(0,1)=(1,−1), we immediately obtain T(2,1)=2(1,1)+(1,−1)=(3,1). Knowing the outputs of the basis vectors determines the output of every vector; a matrix stores exactly that information in its columns.
The attraction of linear algebra is that one small collection of ideas answers several different questions. A system of linear equations asks which inputs produce a prescribed output. The image of a linear map describes the attainable outputs, while the kernel describes the invisible input changes. A basis gives every vector an address, and change of basis lets us choose addresses that make a linear map easier to understand. This shared language turns a collection of separate calculations into a picture of what is possible and how much freedom remains. Gilbert Strang's MIT course emphasizes these connections and their usefulness across other disciplines.[ref]

Hyperbolic pair (B(e,f)=1)

Words: 51
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
Two vectors spanning a hyperbolic plane. For an alternating bilinear form, choose B(e,f)=1; then their span is nondegenerate. For a quadratic form with polar form B, require also Q(e)=Q(f)=0. The analogous definition for a Hermitian form uses two isotropic vectors of pairing one. Extending such pairs to adapted bases is useful for constructing form-preserving maps.

Cartesian basis (E=(e1​,…,en​))

Words: 768 Articles: 3
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A Cartesian basis is an ordered basis of unit vectors along the mutually perpendicular axes of a Cartesian coordinate system. It is an orthonormal basis of a real Euclidean space: ei​⋅ej​=δij​, with δij​ the Kronecker delta. In the plane, the familiar standard basis is e1​=(1,0)T, e2​=(0,1)T; the vector p=(2,1)T is 2e1​+e2​. A rotated pair of perpendicular unit vectors is also a Cartesian basis, even though its basis vectors have different standard basis entries.
The advantage is that coordinates can be measured separately by dot products, and the squared norm is the sum of their squares:
p=∑i​(p⋅ei​)ei​,[p]E​=(p⋅e1​,…,p⋅en​)T,∥p∥2=∑i​(p⋅ei​)2.
(1)
These are the real Euclidean space instances of the orthonormal basis expansion.[ref]
An orthogonal basis only requires perpendicular basis vectors; their lengths need not be one. For example, (2,0)T,(0,3)T are orthogonal, but p=(2,1)T has coordinates (1,1/3)T, while its dot products with them are 4,3. For an orthogonal basis (ai​), the coordinate along ai​ is (p⋅ai​)/(ai​⋅ai​). Dividing each nonzero basis vector by its norm makes it a unit vector without changing its direction. Unit length alone does not imply orthogonality: (1,0)T and (1,1)T/2​ are both unit vectors but have dot product 1/2​.
The examples below show why these distinctions matter: rotating a Cartesian basis changes the coordinate vector while keeping lengths easy to compute; using nonperpendicular basis vectors still gives unique coordinates, but requires the dual basis or a matrix inverse to extract them.

Cartesian basis under rotation ([p]U​=QTp)

Words: 197
Cartesian basis OurBigBook.com
Rotate the standard basis through 30∘ using the rotation matrix whose columns are the new basis vectors:
u=(3​/21/2​),v=(−1/23​/2​),Q=[u v]=(3​/21/2​−1/23​/2​),U=(u,v).
(2)
Here u⋅v=0 and u⋅u=v⋅v=1, so Q is an orthogonal matrix with QTQ=I, where T denotes transpose and I is the identity matrix. For the same vector p=(2,1)T, its coordinate vector in this Cartesian basis is
[p]U​=QTp=(p⋅up⋅v​)=(3​+1/2−1+3​/2​)=(αβ​).
(3)
Thus α≈2.232 and β≈−0.134: travel forwards along u and a little backwards along v to reconstruct p=αu+βv. The orthogonal projections onto the two axes give these signed coordinates because the measuring vectors are both perpendicular and of unit length.
The squared norm remains
α2+β2=(3​+1/2)2+(−1+3​/2)2=(13/4+3​)+(7/4−3​)=5=22+12.
(4)
This is useful when choosing axes aligned with a geometric feature: the coordinates change but distances and dot products retain the same sum-of-products formula. The two directions of the change of basis must be kept straight: Q reconstructs the vector in old coordinates, p=Q[p]U​, and QT extracts its new coordinates. Applying Q to the old coordinate vector p instead would actively rotate the vector.
A short proof explains both formulas. If p=Qc, multiplication by QT gives c=QTp. Then ∥p∥2=cTQTQc=cTc. Perpendicular unit-length columns make the matrix inverse equal the transpose; this is the computational convenience supplied by a Cartesian basis.

Cartesian and oblique coordinate reconstruction (c=B−1p,BTp=Gc)

Words: 229
Cartesian basis OurBigBook.com
Keep the same origin and the same vector p=(2,1)T, but use the nonperpendicular basis vectors b1​=(1,0)T and b2​=(1,1)T. They form a basis because the column matrix B has nonzero determinant:
B=[b1​ b2​]=(10​11​),B−1=(10​−11​),[p]B​=B−1p=(11​).
(5)
The reconstruction is p=b1​+b2​. Its coordinates are read along lines parallel to the other axis, producing a parallelogram. These lines need not be perpendicular to the axis being measured. In contrast, the dot products are p⋅b1​=2 and p⋅b2​=3; treating those as coordinates would reconstruct 2b1​+3b2​=(5,3)T, a different vector.
The dual basis supplies the right measuring rules for any basis.[ref] Here these coordinate functionals are b1∗​(x,y)=x−y and b2∗​(x,y)=y, the rows of B−1. They give b1∗​(p)=b2∗​(p)=1. Equivalently, their representing vectors d1​=(1,−1)T, d2​=(0,1)T satisfy di​⋅bj​=δij​ and extract the coordinates as di​⋅p. These are Riesz dual basis in an inner product space representatives, rather than the original basis vectors.
The Gram matrix records how the nonperpendicular directions interact:
G=BTB=(11​12​),BTp=G[p]B​=(23​),∥p∥2=[p]BT​G[p]B​=5.
(6)
For any real basis represented by a square invertible matrix B, writing p=Bc gives these identities immediately. One can recover the coordinates either as c=B−1p or by solving Gc=BTp. In this example, if c=(a,b)T, the squared norm is a2+2ab+2b2, not a2+b2. Oblique coordinates remain useful when natural directions are not perpendicular, but the Gram matrix must accompany them when computing lengths or dot products.

Cartesian frame (F=(O;e1​,…,en​))

Words: 139
Cartesian basis OurBigBook.com
A Cartesian frame combines a chosen origin point O with a Cartesian basis E, including its ordering as an ordered basis. A point P has coordinate vector c when OP=∑i​ci​ei​. The basis supplies measuring directions and unit lengths; the coordinate vector is the resulting tuple of numbers; the Cartesian frame additionally fixes where measurement starts. A vector already belongs to a vector space with a zero vector, so expressing it in a basis requires no additional choice of spatial origin.
For example, keeping the standard basis but moving the origin from O=(0,0) to O′=(1,0) changes the coordinates of the physical point P=(2,1) from (2,1)T to (1,1)T. This happens because O′P=OP−OO′ is a different displacement vector. By contrast, the two diagrams above keep O fixed and change only the basis. In a fixed reference Cartesian frame, a new frame with origin column o and basis-column matrix Q describes points by p=o+Qc; the new coordinates are c=QT(p−o) when Q is an orthogonal matrix.

Sesquilinear form

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A sesquilinear form on a complex vector space V is a map B:V×V→C which, with the convention used throughout this article, is a linear map in its first argument and a conjugate-linear map in its second. For vectors u,v,w and complex numbers α,β, the defining identities are
B(αu+βv,w)=αB(u,w)+βB(v,w),B(u,αv+βw)=αB(u,v)+β​B(u,w).
(7)
The bars denote complex conjugation. No symmetry or positivity is required. Some authors choose the opposite convention; every formula here keeps the first argument linear.[ref]
For a basis e1​,…,en​ of a finite-dimensional vector space, write u=∑i​xi​ei​, v=∑j​yj​ej​, and Aij​=B(ei​,ej​). Expanding by the two identities gives
B(u,v)=∑i,j​xi​Aij​yj​​=xTAy​.
(8)
Every complex matrix A gives a sesquilinear form this way. The superscript T means transpose, not conjugate transpose. Equivalently, the scalar is y∗ATx, where y∗=y​T. This is the convention used for the matrix of a Hermitian form when symmetry is imposed. The coordinate formula follows directly by expanding the basis coefficients.[ref]
For a concrete example on C2, let B(z,w)=z1​w2​​. Its matrix is (00​10​): B(e1​,e2​)=1 but B(e2​,e1​)=0, so it is not a Hermitian form. Also B((1,i),(1,i))=−i, so even real diagonal values cannot be assumed for an arbitrary sesquilinear form. By comparison, the bilinear form F(z,w)=z1​w1​+z2​w2​ satisfies F(iz,w)=F(z,iw)=iF(z,w) and has F((i,0),(i,0))=−1; it cannot supply positive squared lengths on this complex vector space.
The effect of changing the complex argument of a multiplier is particularly revealing. For real numbers θ,ϕ, sesquilinear forms satisfy
B(eiθu,eiϕv)=ei(θ−ϕ)B(u,v),B(αu,αu)=∣α∣2B(u,u).
(9)
Thus a common change of complex argument cancels from the diagonal, whereas the two arguments rotate the output in opposite directions. Conjugating one argument is what replaces the α2 scaling of a bilinear form by the nonnegative ∣α∣2 scaling needed for a Hermitian inner product. This mechanism also works in function spaces: for complex continuous functions on [0,1], B(f,g)=∫01​f(t)g(t)​dt obeys the same identities, letting integration measure overlap rather than merely multiply coefficients.

A Hermitian form is a sesquilinear form on a complex vector space satisfying conjugate symmetry,
H(w,v)=H(v,w)​.
(10)
Hence q(v)=H(v,v) is a real number for every vector. In a basis, the matrix of a Hermitian form has Aij​=H(ei​,ej​) and obeys Aji​=Aij​​, equivalently A=A∗: it is a Hermitian matrix. The coordinate rule remains H(x,y)=xTAy​. Conjugate symmetry does not imply positivity.[ref]
The diagonal contains more information than might be expected. For any complex sesquilinear form B, put q(v)=B(v,v). Expanding four expressions gives the complex polarization identity in the linear-first convention:
B(u,v)=41​(q(u+v)−q(u−v)+iq(u+iv)−iq(u−iv)).
(11)
This is an algebraic identity, with no positivity assumption. If every q(v) is real, interchanging u,v preserves the first difference and negates the second: use q(αv)=∣α∣2q(v) for α=−1,i. The identity then gives B(v,u)=B(u,v)​. Thus a complex sesquilinear form is a Hermitian form if and only if all its diagonal values are real. Testing only the basis vectors is insufficient: the off-diagonal example in sesquilinear form has zero diagonal entries in its matrix but a nonreal value at (1,i).
Consider the indefinite Hermitian form
H−​(z,w)=z1​w1​​−z2​w2​​,q−​(z)=∣z1​∣2−∣z2​∣2.
(12)
Its values at e1​,e2​ are 1,−1. Moreover u=(1,1) and v=(1,−1) are nonzero isotropic vectors: q−​(u)=q−​(v)=0, yet H−​(u,v)=2. These vectors do not belong to the radical of a Hermitian form, and the usual Cauchy-Schwarz inequality would incorrectly require 4≤0. An indefinite Hermitian form records signed geometry rather than defining a norm by H(v,v)​.
There is a separate boundary case: H0​(z,w)=z1​w1​​ is a positive semidefinite Hermitian form, since H0​(z,z)=∣z1​∣2≥0, but H0​(e2​,e2​)=0. Its radical of a Hermitian form is the entire second coordinate line. Positive definiteness is exactly the additional condition in a Hermitian inner product. The three examples below show why these distinctions matter: on the real slice z=(x,y)∈R2⊂C2, q+​(z)=∣z1​∣2+2∣z2​∣2 has an ellipse as its unit level, q−​ has hyperbolas, and q0​ has two parallel lines. These are slices of the complex examples, not drawings of their full four-dimensional domains.

Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
A Hermitian inner product is a Hermitian form H on a complex vector space which has positive definiteness: H(v,v)>0 for every nonzero vector v. It is precisely a complex inner product. Only with this definiteness condition does
∥v∥=H(v,v)​
(13)
define a norm rather than a seminorm or an expression that may not be real. The standard Hermitian inner product on Cn is H(z,w)=∑j​zj​wj​​; positive weights cj​ give ∑j​cj​zj​wj​​, with squared norm ∑j​cj​∣zj​∣2.[ref]
A Hermitian inner product need not have a real matrix. For instance, with the linear-first coordinate convention,
A=(2−i​i2​),H(z,w)=zTAw,H(z,z)=∣z1​−iz2​∣2+∣z1​∣2+∣z2​∣2.

The last expression proves positive definiteness without a lengthy calculation of eigenvalues. For z=(1,i) it gives 6, while for z=(1,−i) it gives 2. These unequal values expose why a silent switch to z∗Az would change this particular Hermitian inner product: with these same entries it gives 2 at (1,i). All entries must keep their roles from the matrix of a Hermitian form.
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for a Hermitian inner product states
∣H(v,u)∣2≤H(v,v)H(u,u).
(15)
Equality holds exactly when u,v are linearly dependent, including when either is zero. For a nonzero u, outline the proof by setting a=H(v,u)/H(u,u) and r=v−au. Then H(r,u)=0, and the Pythagorean theorem gives
H(v,v)=H(u,u)∣H(v,u)∣2​+H(r,r).
(16)
Nonnegativity proves the inequality, while positive definiteness makes equality equivalent to r=0. The scalar a has no extra conjugate because the first argument is linear.[ref]
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality also holds for a positive semidefinite Hermitian form, but equality need not imply linear dependence: for H0​(z,w)=z1​w1​​, the independent vectors e1​ and e1​+e2​ give 1=1. Equality then describes dependence after passing to the quotient vector space by the radical of a Hermitian form. The indefinite Hermitian form in Hermitian form shows that conjugate symmetry alone does not even guarantee the inequality.
For a worked orthogonal projection, take H+​(z,w)=z1​w1​​+2z2​w2​​, u=(1,1) and v=(2,0). Then a=2/3, au=(2/3,2/3) and r=(4/3,−2/3), with H+​(r,u)=0 and 4=4/3+8/3 for the squared norms. The residual is perpendicular in this Hermitian inner product even though its ordinary real dot product with u is 2/3. For complex v=(1,i), the same orthogonal projection uses a=(1+2i)/3; rotating v multiplies a by eiθ, while rotating u multiplies a by e−iθ. This combines geometric decomposition with sensitivity to the relative complex arguments of the multipliers.
A Hermitian inner product therefore supplies more than a positive diagonal: orthogonality, orthogonal projection onto a span, and the triangle inequality for its norm make approximation and distance meaningful. For the function space of complex continuous functions on [0,1], H(f,g)=∫01​f(t)g(t)​dt has positive definiteness, because a nonzero continuous function has positive modulus on a small interval. The same construction turns overlap under integration into lengths and best approximation in finite-dimensional vector subspaces.

Radical of a Hermitian form (radh={v:h(v,w)=0 for all w})

Words: 65
Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
The radical of a Hermitian form is the vector subspace orthogonal to the entire space. The form descends to the quotient vector space by its radical: adding a radical vector to either argument does not change the value. For a positive semidefinite Hermitian form, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality identifies this radical with its zero-norm vectors, so the quotient form is positive definite. This conclusion does not hold for a general indefinite Hermitian form: a zero-norm vector need not belong to its radical.

Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
A Hermitian form is positive semidefinite when h(v,v)≥0 for every vector. It need not define an inner product, because a nonzero vector may have zero squared norm. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality still holds: applying nonnegativity to v+zw and minimizing the quadratic expression in z gives ∣h(v,w)∣2≤h(v,v)h(w,w) when h(w,w)>0; when h(w,w)=0, varying z forces h(v,w)=0. Thus its zero-norm vectors are exactly the radical of a Hermitian form. Quotienting this radical of a Hermitian form gives a positive inner product; taking its Hilbert space completion then gives a Hilbert space. This is the final positivity step in the Gupta-Bleuler null-state quotient.

Singular value decomposition (A=UΣV∗)

Words: 988 Articles: 4
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
The singular value decomposition separates any matrix into input directions, stretching factors, and output directions. Every m×n complex matrix admits
A=UΣV∗,U∈Cm×m,Σ∈Rm×n,V∈Cn×n.
(17)
Here U,V are unitary matrices, V∗=V† is the conjugate transpose, and Σ is a rectangular diagonal matrix. Its p=min(m,n) diagonal entries are the singular values, ordered σ1​≥⋯≥σp​≥0. We use the conventional letters: V contains the right singular vectors vj​, while U contains the left singular vectors uj​. Writing A=VΣU† instead merely swaps these two matrix names; it requires swapping their roles consistently. For real matrices, choose orthogonal matrices and replace the conjugate transpose with the transpose.[ref]
Reading from right to left, V∗ expresses the input in an orthonormal basis, Σ stretches or annihilates those coordinates, and U assembles the output in another orthonormal basis. Unlike matrix similarity, the input and output bases can differ, and even have different sizes. A 3×2 matrix has full factors of sizes 3×3, 3×2, and 2×2. If its matrix rank is 2, one can retain only the active columns, giving sizes 3×2, 2×2, and 2×2 for Ur​,Σr​,Vr∗​; the full U additionally describes an unused output direction.
For a fully computed nonsymmetric example, take
A=(3−4/5​43/5​),U=I,Σ=(50​01​),V=51​(34​−43​).
(18)
Multiplication gives UΣVT=A. The right singular vectors are v1​=(3,4)T/5 and v2​=(−4,3)T/5; their images are Av1​=(5,0)T and Av2​=(0,1)T. Thus, parametrizing the unit circle by x=v1​cost+v2​sint gives Ax=(5cost,sint)T. Its image is the ellipse y12​/25+y22​=1. The two singular values are its semiaxis lengths, and the left singular vectors point along its axes. The singular value decomposition finds precisely the perpendicular input directions whose images stay perpendicular.
For compression, write the matrix as a sum of outer products and retain the largest terms:
A=∑j=1r​σj​uj​vj∗​,Ak​=∑j=1k​σj​uj​vj∗​,∥A−Ak​∥F2​=∑j=k+1r​σj2​,
(19)
where r is the matrix rank. Among all matrices of matrix rank at most k, Ak​ minimizes the Frobenius norm error; this is the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. The operator norm error is σk+1​ for k<r. These statements concern specified norms, rather than guaranteeing that discarded details are visually or scientifically unimportant.[ref]
Consider an 8×10 brightness matrix B=pqT+abT/2, with
p=(1,2,3,4,4,3,2,1)T,q=(1,2,3,4,5,5,4,3,2,1)T,
(20)
and ai​=(−1)i−1, bj​=(−1)j−1. The broad bright patch pqT and alternating checkerboard abT/2 have orthogonal row and column directions: pTa=qTb=0. Their singular values are 60⋅110​=6600​ and 8⋅10​/2=20​. This low-rank approximation keeps the first outer product, giving B1​=pqT, with Frobenius norm error 20​≈4.472 and relative error 20/6620​≈5.50%. For example, B11​=1.5 becomes 1, and B12​=1.5 becomes 2: every entry changes by 0.5 in magnitude. The discarded pattern is small but entirely lost.
For this illustrative image compression, storing one normalized left singular vector, one normalized right singular vector, and one singular value requires 8+10+1=19 scalars instead of 80. This counts scalars at equal precision, before storage overhead. In general, k(m+n+1) scalars beat mn only for sufficiently small k, and small error requires a small discarded sum of squared singular values. The usefulness comes from measuring the tradeoff before throwing information away.[ref]

ATA=251​(241288​288409​),AAT=(250​01​).

Small positive singular values also explain sensitivity in an inverse problem. For a square invertible matrix, the matrix inverse sends uj​ to vj​/σj​: a weak forward response becomes strong inverse amplification. The condition number for Euclidean norm is σ1​/σn​, equal to 5 in our example. To see a larger effect, keep the same right singular vectors but change the second singular value to ε=0.01:

Singular value OurBigBook.com
A right singular vector vj​ is a unit vector in the input space satisfying A∗Avj​=σj2​vj​. For positive singular values, Avj​=σj​uj​ determines the matching left singular vector. In the ellipse example, Av1​=(5,0)T is not parallel to v1​: a right singular vector need not be an eigenvector of A. Indeed, the characteristic polynomial of A is λ2−(18/5)λ+5, with eigenvalues (9±i44​)/5 and no real eigenvectors. Nevertheless, its real right singular vectors give a complete orthonormal basis. Eigenvectors describe preserved directions; right singular vectors describe orthogonal input channels of stretching.[ref]
An arbitrary input mixes these channels. For x=c1​v1​+c2​v2​, orthogonality gives ∥Ax∥22​=25∣c1​∣2+∣c2​∣2, while ∥x∥22​=∣c1​∣2+∣c2​∣2. Equal contributions, c1​=c2​=1/2​, produce output Euclidean norm 13​ from a unit vector. Concentrating the entire input along v1​ produces the maximum 5. This is why the right singular vectors give a direct reading of how any input will behave. For a compact operator, the same definition describes the positive terms of its singular value system.

Left singular vector (uj​)

Words: 117
Singular value OurBigBook.com
A left singular vector uj​ is a unit vector in the output space satisfying AA∗uj​=σj2​uj​. For positive singular values, the pairing also satisfies A∗uj​=σj​vj​. Thus u1​=(1,0)T and u2​=(0,1)T describe the output axes of the preceding ellipse, while the right singular vectors describe its input directions. At zero singular values, division by σj​ is impossible: complete the orthonormal bases independently in the null spaces of A and A∗. Repeated singular values allow different matched orthonormal bases within the corresponding eigenspaces. The same positive pairing extends to a compact operator through its singular value system.
Even distinct singular values do not fix arrow signs: replacing both uj​ and vj​ by their negatives preserves Avj​=σj​uj​ and the outer product uj​vj∗​. Reversing only one arrow would change that term's sign. The paired directions, rather than independently chosen arrow orientations, encode the matrix.

Low-rank approximation (minrankB≤r​∥A−B∥)

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A low-rank approximation replaces an m×n matrix A by a matrix B of matrix rank at most a chosen integer r, with 0≤r≤min(m,n), while making an explicitly chosen error norm small. The point is to describe many entries using a few shared patterns: an image compression may retain broad brightness patterns while discarding finer ones. The approximation is useful when the saved storage or computation justifies the lost detail. A small matrix rank alone says nothing about the error.
The compact representation is a sum of outer products, equivalently a product of two thin matrices:
B=XY∗=∑j=1r​xj​yj∗​,X∈Cm×r,Y∈Cn×r.
(24)
Here xj​,yj​ are the columns of X,Y, and the star denotes the conjugate transpose; over the real numbers use the transpose. The rank bound for a matrix product gives rankB≤r. Conversely, choose a basis of the column space of B as the columns of X, and put the coordinates of each column of B into Y∗; pad with zero columns if the matrix rank is smaller than r. Each nonzero outer product is a rank-one matrix: it repeats a single column pattern at different strengths across the columns.
Keeping the two factors stores r(m+n) scalars instead of mn. This saves space only when r(m+n)<mn. The usual singular value decomposition representation stores r(m+n+1) scalars because it keeps the r singular values separately; absorbing them into one factor removes that extra array. These are representation sizes at equal scalar precision, before file overhead. See Uschmajew and Vandereycken, §9.2: thin factors and their storage, and Illinois CS 357, Low-rank approximation: storing singular vectors and values.
The factors also give Bz=X(Y∗z) without forming the full matrix B. Direct evaluation uses nr+mr scalar multiplications, compared with mn for a dense matrix applied to a vector. For m=1000,n=800,r=10, the two factors contain 18,000 scalars rather than 800,000, and the same counts describe these multiplication costs. Constructing the factors is a separate cost. Moreover, a low-rank approximation need not be a sparse matrix: the constant 8×8 matrix whose entries are all 1 has matrix rank 1 despite having no zero entries.
For the standard unweighted problem, write a singular value decomposition with p=min(m,n) and singular values σ1​≥⋯≥σp​≥0. Retain the first r paired left singular vectors and right singular vectors:
Ar​=∑j=1r​σj​uj​vj∗​,A0​=0.
(25)
The Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem says that this same Ar​ minimizes both of the following error norms over all matrices with matrix rank at most r:
minrankB≤r​∥A−B∥F​=∥A−Ar​∥F​=(∑j=r+1p​σj2​)1/2,minrankB≤r​∥A−B∥2​=∥A−Ar​∥2​=σr+1​,
(26)
where σp+1​=0 and an empty sum is zero. Here the Frobenius norm is ∥E∥F​=(∑i,j​∣Eij​∣2)1/2, whereas the operator norm is specifically induced by the Euclidean norm, ∥E∥2​=max∥z∥2​=1​∥Ez∥2​. The first aggregates errors in all entries; the second bounds the worst output error for a unit vector input. These formulas apply to real and complex matrices. [ref]
For A=0, a relative Frobenius norm tolerance ε is met precisely when the discarded squared singular values sum to at most ε2∑j​σj2​. Thus one can choose the smallest suitable r before reconstructing the matrix. Many individually small discarded singular values can still have a large combined error. An operator norm tolerance instead tests only the largest discarded singular value, σr+1​. The two questions can therefore select different ranks.
The following stipulated 8×8 matrix makes the tradeoff visible. Define four real vectors of length 8:
h0​=(1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1)T,h1​=(1,1,1,1,−1,−1,−1,−1)T,
(27)
h2​=(1,1,−1,−1,1,1,−1,−1)T,h3​=(1,−1,1,−1,1,−1,1,−1)T,A=h0​h0T​+83​h1​h1T​+81​h2​h2T​+161​h3​h3T​.
(28)
The vectors hj​/8​ are orthonormal, so this is already a singular value decomposition written as outer products, with positive singular values 8,3,1,1/2. All entries lie between 7/16 and 25/16 and can be displayed as brightnesses. The first component is uniform brightness, the second distinguishes broad blocks, and the last two supply finer alternating patterns. This is a designed arithmetic example, not measured image data.
Here A1​=h0​h0T​ has every entry equal to 1, while A2​=h0​h0T​+3h1​h1T​/8 has entries 11/8 within the two diagonal blocks and 5/8 in the other two blocks. For instance, A11​=25/16 becomes (A2​)11​=11/8: its error is 3/16. The full residual is h2​h2T​/8+h3​h3T​/16, whose Frobenius norm is 1+(1/2)2​=5​/2 and whose operator norm is 1. Since ∥A∥F​=297​/2, the relative Frobenius norm error is 5/297​≈12.97%. Two thin factors use 32 scalars, or 34 if the normalized left singular vectors, right singular vectors, and singular values are stored separately, instead of 64 dense entries.
Retaining three components reduces the Frobenius norm error to 1/2 while using 48 scalars in two factors. Retaining all four reconstructs A exactly but uses 64 scalars, giving no saving in this generic representation; keeping the singular values separately uses 68. Our particular sign patterns could be encoded more economically, but that would exploit an additional structure beyond the general low-rank approximation. The striking feature is that numerical error and storage can both be read from the decomposition, rather than judged only by how smooth the picture looks.
The constraint is deliberately matrix rank at most r. The truncation has rankAr​=min(r,rankA). If rankA<r, the best approximation is A itself, with zero error. Requiring matrix rank exactly r can destroy attainment: for A=diag(1,0) and r=2, the matrices Bδ​=diag(1,δ) have matrix rank 2 for δ>0, and both error norms equal δ. Their error has infimum zero, but no rank-two matrix attains it. If r≤rankA, the displayed Ar​ does have matrix rank exactly r and attains the same minimum under either constraint.
Optimality also does not always mean uniqueness. For 0<r<rankA, the best Frobenius norm approximation is unique when σr​>σr+1​. [ref] A positive tie across the cutoff permits different choices: for A=diag(3,3,1) and r=1, both diag(3,0,0) and diag(0,3,0) have Frobenius norm error 10​ and operator norm error 3. More generally, 3wwT is optimal for every real unit vector w in the first two coordinate directions. Rotating which tied direction is kept changes the approximation. Repeated singular values entirely inside the retained group do not change its sum of outer products. At r=0 the only feasible matrix is zero; at r≥rankA the unique zero-error approximation is A, even if some singular values are tied at zero.
A strict gap does not guarantee uniqueness for the operator norm. For A=diag(3,1) and r=1, every Bt​=diag(t,0) with 2≤t≤4 has matrix rank 1 and error ∥A−Bt​∥2​=max(∣3−t∣,1)=1, which is optimal. Only t=3 minimizes the Frobenius norm, since ∥A−Bt​∥F​=(3−t)2+1​. An unchanged worst direction can hide extra error in another direction under the operator norm.
Finally, these guarantees concern the stated norms and the sole matrix rank constraint. They do not establish that a discarded pattern is noise or irrelevant to a particular task: the finer patterns in our constructed example were put there intentionally. Adding entrywise weights or restrictions on the factors changes the problem, so the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem above does not automatically solve it. For historical context, the original 1936 matrix problem is documented in the existing Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem section.

For a finite matrix with singular values in nonincreasing order, truncating its singular value decomposition after k terms minimizes the Frobenius norm error, whose square is the sum of the discarded squared singular values. It also minimizes the operator norm error, which equals the next singular value, or zero if none remain. See Mazeika, Section 4.3: Low rank approximation.
The problem of replacing a matrix by one of lower matrix rank is explicit in Eckart and Young's 1936 paper, [ref]. The publication predates the modern image compression example, showing how a general matrix question can support later applications.

Unimodular matrix (U∈GLn​(Z))

Words: 673 Articles: 3
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A unimodular matrix is a square integer matrix whose determinant is 1 or −1. The decisive property is that its inverse matrix also has integer entries: multiplication by U gives a bijection of the integer lattice Zn onto itself. Thus an invertible linear map can preserve not only real coordinates but the requirement that every coordinate is an integer. These matrices form the integral general linear group.[ref]
For an original two-dimensional example, take
U=(10​11​),U−1=(10​−11​).
(29)
Its determinant is one, and it maps (a,b) to (a+b,b). Conversely, the integer point (x,y) comes from (x−y,y). For instance, (3,2) has new coordinates (1,2) relative to the columns (1,0) and (1,1). No integer point disappears, although the basis vectors and their fundamental cell change shape.
This is useful whenever coordinates must remain integral. A unimodular change of lattice basis can give a shorter or more convenient description without changing the objects represented. Smith normal form and Hermite normal form use controlled integer operations to simplify integer matrices; ordinary Gaussian elimination may divide by numbers that destroy integrality. The geometric freedom is substantial: a sheared basis may look completely different while describing exactly the same infinite set of integer points.
A determinant of −1 is allowed too. Swapping two basis columns reverses orientation while preserving the integer lattice. The condition is therefore preservation of the complete integer structure, rather than a requirement to preserve orientation.

Integer inverse criterion for a unimodular matrix (U∈Zn×n,U−1∈Zn×n⟺detU=±1)

Words: 79
Unimodular matrix OurBigBook.com
For a square integer matrix U with nonzero determinant, the inverse matrix has integer entries exactly when detU=±1. The adjugate matrix formula proves one direction:
U−1=detUadj(U)​.
(30)
Every entry of adj(U) is an integer cofactor, so division by 1 or −1 leaves integer entries. Conversely, if both U and U−1 are integer matrices, their determinants are integers with product one. The only possibilities are that both are one or both are minus one. This explains why a general integer matrix with nonzero determinant need not have an integer inverse matrix.

Unimodular change of lattice basis (B2​=B1​U,U∈GLn​(Z))

Words: 125
Unimodular matrix OurBigBook.com
Let B1​,B2​ be real square invertible matrices whose columns are lattice bases. They generate the same Euclidean lattice precisely when
B1​Zn=B2​Zn⟺B2​=B1​U for a unimodular matrix U.​
(31)
[ref]
If B2​=B1​U, multiplication by U merely permutes the integer coordinate vectors, so the two generated sets agree. Conversely, equality of the generated sets means every column of either basis is an integer linear combination of the other. Hence B2​=B1​U and B1​=B2​V for integer matrices U,V. Substitution followed by multiplication by B1−1​ gives UV=I, so the integer inverse criterion for a unimodular matrix applies.
Equal real linear spans are a weaker condition: any two real square invertible matrices span the same ambient vector space. Even equal covolumes do not force the same Euclidean lattice. The requirement that the change matrix and its inverse matrix have integer entries provides the missing arithmetic information.

Integer determinant and sublattice index ([Zn:AZn]=∣detA∣)

Words: 214
Unimodular matrix OurBigBook.com
For a square integer matrix A with nonzero determinant, the image AZn is a subgroup of the integer lattice. Its index of a subgroup is
[Zn:AZn]=∣detA∣.
(32)
In particular, A=diag(2,1) gives all points with even first coordinate. The quotient has two cosets, represented by (0,0) and (1,0), and the fundamental cell has area two. A determinant of two therefore counts how much integer information is missing from the image.
The integrality hypothesis is essential. The rational matrix R=diag(2,1/2) has determinant one but sends (0,1) to (0,1/2). Its generated Euclidean lattice has the same covolume as Z2 without being the same integer lattice. The unimodular matrix criterion combines an arithmetic condition with a geometric one.
A short proof of the index formula uses Smith normal form. Write PAQ=diag(d1​,…,dn​), with P,Q unimodular matrices and positive integers di​. They preserve the relevant integer structure, so the quotient has the same size as ∏i​Z/di​Z, namely ∏i​di​=∣detA∣. No assumption that the matrix is orthogonal or its basis vectors are short is needed.

Householder transformation (H=I−2uuT)

Words: 723 Articles: 3
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A Householder transformation is a reflection that leaves every direction in a chosen hyperplane fixed and reverses its normal direction. For a real unit vector u, its matrix is
H=I−2uuT.​
(33)
To understand the formula, decompose any vector into its orthogonal projection onto the normal and a perpendicular component:
x=x∥​+x⊥​,x∥​=(uTx)u,uTx⊥​=0.
(34)
Then Hx=x⊥​−x∥​. Subtracting twice the normal component changes its sign while retaining everything parallel to the mirror. A nonzero normal v gives the equivalent formula H=I−2vvT/(vTv), so normalization can be deferred.
For example, take u=(2,1)T/5​. Its mirror is the straight line 2x1​+x2​=0, and
H=(−3/5−4/5​−4/53/5​),H(34​)=(−50​).
(35)
The midpoint of these two vectors is (−1,2)T, which lies on the mirror; their connecting segment is parallel to its normal. Both vectors have Euclidean norm five.
Several useful properties follow from this decomposition. The Householder reflection is a symmetric matrix and an orthogonal matrix:
HT=H,H2=I,HTH=I.
(36)
Reflecting twice restores the original vector; Euclidean norms and inner products are preserved. The eigenvalue is −1 along u and +1 on u⊥, so detH=−1. A reflection reverses orientation even though it preserves lengths.
The computational payoff is that the mirror can be chosen to send a whole vector onto one coordinate axis, eliminating several entries at once. Householder QR decomposition repeats this operation on the remaining parts of successive columns. For a real symmetric matrix, applying the same Householder reflection on both sides gives a matrix similarity HAH that preserves symmetry and eigenvalues; this is the basis of Householder tridiagonalization.
Alston S. Householder's 1958 paper Unitary Triangularization of a Nonsymmetric Matrix develops this elimination method. Its motivation includes reducing the arithmetic needed for triangularization while retaining the conditioning advantages of orthogonal transformations. [ref] Over the complex numbers, I−2uu∗ for a unit u is Hermitian and unitary, with the star denoting the conjugate transpose; the coordinate-axis construction below is stated for real vectors.

Commuting plane reflections (Hb​Ha​−Ha​Hb​=4(a⋅b)(baT−abT))

Words: 99
Householder transformation OurBigBook.com
For real unit vectors a,b, the Householder reflections Ha​=I−2aaT and Hb​=I−2bbT commute exactly when their normals are parallel or orthogonal. Expanding their products proves the formula. If a⋅b=0, a zero commutator requires baT=abT; applying this identity to a gives b=(a⋅b)a, hence parallelism. Orthogonal normals make the prefactor zero.
Equality on one selected vector is weaker than equality of the operators. For nonparallel, nonorthogonal normals in three dimensions, the commutator's kernel is the line perpendicular to both normals, spanned by a×b. A vector on that line is fixed by both reflections even though the operators do not commute.

α={−∥x∥2​,∥x∥2​,​x1​≥0,x1​<0.​

Change of basis

Words: 399 Articles: 2
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A change of basis rewrites a vector using a different ordered basis of the same vector space. The vector stays fixed; its coordinate vector changes because the measuring directions change. Both bases must describe every vector uniquely, so a change of basis is reversible.
Start with the Cartesian basis e1​=(1,0), e2​=(0,1), and choose the new basis vectors u=(1,1) and v=(1,−1). For the vector z=(2,0),
z=2e1​+0e2​=u+v,[z]old​=(20​),[z]new​=(11​).
(43)
The second coordinate vector says to travel once along u and once along v. Their vertical contributions cancel, leaving exactly the original horizontal arrow. The diagram shows two descriptions of that same arrow, with the same origin and endpoint.
Choosing a useful basis can reveal simple structure hidden by the old coordinate vectors. Here the new basis describes common and opposing contributions. For two equal measurements (5,5), the new coordinate vector is (5,0): only the common contribution is present. In larger examples, a suitable basis can concentrate important information into a few coefficients. Strang's lecture on change of basis develops this principle through applications: the reversible change of basis preserves information, while subsequently discarding small coefficients loses information.[ref]

Orthogonal change of coordinates (x=Qy,QTQ=I)

Change of basis OurBigBook.com
An orthogonal change of coordinates relates two orthonormal bases of a real inner product space. With the new basis vectors as columns of an orthogonal matrix Q, old and new coordinate columns obey x=Qy. Then xTx=yTy, so Euclidean norm, Euclidean distance and angles are preserved. A quadratic form xTAx becomes yT(QTAQ)y. For a symmetric matrix, orthogonal diagonalization chooses Q so that the transformed quadratic form is a sum of eigenvalues times squared coordinates. This explains the principal-axis descriptions of a quadric surface.

Fix the convention: the columns of the change-of-basis matrix P are the new basis vectors written in the old basis. Thus P converts new coordinate vectors into old ones; its matrix inverse converts old coordinate vectors into new ones. For the preceding basis,
P=(11​1−1​),P−1=21​(11​1−1​),P−1(20​)=(11​).
(44)
Its determinant is −2, so P is an invertible matrix. Checking which direction P converts is essential: different books may call either P or P−1 the change-of-basis matrix.
For a linear operator, convert the input into the old basis, apply the old matrix, and convert the output back. Reading that sequence from right to left gives
Anew​=P−1Aold​P.

For example, let the old diagonal matrix stretch horizontal components by 2 and vertical components by 3. Then
Aold​=(20​03​),Anew​=(2.5−0.5​−0.52.5​),Anew​(11​)=(22​).
(46)
The output represents 2u+2v=(4,0), just as Aold​(2,0)T=(4,0)T. The matrices look different because their bases differ, but they encode the same linear operator. This relation is called matrix similarity; it preserves the underlying action.[ref]

Circulant matrix (Cnj​=c(n−j)modN​)

Words: 726 Articles: 2
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A circulant matrix applies the same rule at every position of a finite ring: moving both the input and output indices one step leaves its entries unchanged. Its first column determines the whole matrix. For a length-N vector c, index rows and columns by 0,…,N−1 and define
Cnj​=c(n−j)modN​.
(47)
The indices use modular arithmetic. Thus each column is the previous column shifted down one place, with the last entry wrapping around to the top. Multiplication is exactly circular convolution:
(Cx)n​=∑j=0N−1​c(n−j)modN​xj​=∑ℓ=0N−1​cℓ​x(n−ℓ)modN​.
(48)
This makes a circulant matrix a natural model for a periodic finite difference rule or a filter acting on a periodic record. Strang's MIT lecture develops this connection between circulant matrices, circular convolution and the discrete Fourier transform.[ref]
For example, the first column c=(2,−1,0,−1)T gives
L=​2−10−1​−12−10​0−12−1​−10−12​​,(Lx)n​=2xn​−xn−1​−xn+1​.
(49)
Here the indices wrap around modulo four. Each output compares a value with its two neighbors; this is the Graph Laplacian of a four-vertex cycle graph. A constant input gives zero, while an alternating input gives a large response. The Fourier diagonalization of a circulant matrix makes this distinction exact: its four eigenvalues are 0,2,4,2.
The plotted discrete Fourier modes are complex vectors, shown through their real and imaginary parts. Each entry has modulus one; the Euclidean norm of each length-four vector is two. In particular, modes k=1 and k=3 have the same real part but opposite imaginary parts, so they are distinct eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue.
The useful surprise is that every length-N circulant matrix shares the same basis of eigenvectors, whatever its first column. One change of basis therefore simplifies an entire family of linear maps, instead of requiring a separate eigenvalue computation for each one. Bamieh's tutorial develops the discrete Fourier transform from precisely this simultaneous diagonalization problem.[ref]

Use the negative-exponential forward discrete Fourier transform and the 1/N-normalized inverse discrete Fourier transform:
Fkn​=e−2πikn/N,(F−1)nk​=N1​e2πink/N.
(50)
For the circulant matrix with first column c, the discrete Fourier mode wn(k)​=e2πikn/N is an eigenvector with eigenvalue
λk​=ℓ=0∑N−1​cℓ​e−2πikℓ/N=(Fc)k​.​
(51)
Indeed, substitution into circular convolution gives
(Cw(k))n​=∑ℓ=0N−1​cℓ​e2πik(n−ℓ)/N=wn(k)​λk​.
(52)
The columns of F−1 are w(k)/N, so the diagonalization of a matrix takes the form
C=F−1diag(λ0​,…,λN−1​)F.
(53)
The roots of unity give orthogonality of these eigenvectors; dividing each w(k) by N​ makes the basis orthonormal. Consequently, every complex circulant matrix is a normal matrix, including ones that are not Hermitian matrices.
The sign convention matters. For c=(1,2,0,0)T, the circulant matrix is
C=​1200​0120​0012​2001​​,(λ0​,λ1​,λ2​,λ3​)=(3,1−2i,−1,1+2i).
(54)
Changing the direction of the shift or the sign in the discrete Fourier transform changes which complex eigenvalue goes with which discrete Fourier mode. A real symmetric example alone would conceal that distinction.
For a linear system Cx=b, put x=Fx and b=Fb. The equation becomes N independent scalar equations
λk​xk​=bk​.
(55)
If every λk​ is nonzero, divide to find the unique vector x and apply the inverse discrete Fourier transform. If some λk​=0, a vector x satisfying the linear system exists exactly when bk​=0 at every such index; the corresponding xk​ remain free. This is a concrete version of the Fredholm alternative in a finite-dimensional setting.
With an appropriate Fast Fourier transform, multiplication or a compatible solve takes O(NlogN) arithmetic operations, instead of forming a dense matrix and applying general Gaussian elimination. The gain comes from the periodic structure; an arbitrary matrix does not have this shared basis of discrete Fourier modes.[ref]

Invertible matrix (rankA=n⟺detA=0)

Words: 737 Articles: 3
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
An n-by-n square matrix A over a field is invertible when it has a two-sided matrix inverse. Equivalently, its linear map x↦Ax is a bijection: every output comes from exactly one input. For a square matrix, the following conditions are equivalent:
A is invertible⟺rankA=n⟺kerA={0}⟺detA=0⟺Ax=b has exactly one solution for every b.
(59)
Here matrix rank n means both full column rank and full row rank. The square hypothesis matters: a rectangular matrix can have full column rank without reaching every output, or full row rank without determining every input.[ref]
The equivalences explain why invertibility is a question about retaining information. A trivial kernel makes the linear map injective; the rank-nullity theorem then gives matrix rank n, so its columns form a basis and the linear map is also surjective. Assigning to each output its unique input gives a linear map: the preimage of αb+βc is αA−1b+βA−1c. The determinant is nonzero precisely when the columns are linearly independent. Thus algebraic solvability and independent directions describe the same phenomenon; over the real numbers, nonzero oriented volume supplies its geometric interpretation.

Quadratic lower bound for a nonsymmetric matrix (xTBx≥c∣x∣2⟹∣Bx∣≥c∣x∣,c>0)

Invertible matrix OurBigBook.com
Let B be a real square matrix and suppose xTBx≥c∣x∣2 for every real vector x, with c>0. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives xTBx≤∣x∣∣Bx∣, hence ∣Bx∣≥c∣x∣ for all x. In particular the kernel is zero, so B is an invertible matrix. Applying the bound to x=B−1y gives the operator norm estimate ∥B−1∥≤1/c in the Euclidean norm.
Symmetry of B is unnecessary: xTBx=xTHx for its symmetric part of a matrix H=(B+BT)/2. Thus the hypothesis is exactly a positive lower bound on that symmetric matrix, even when the antisymmetric part is nonzero.

Singular matrix

Words: 493 Articles: 1
Invertible matrix OurBigBook.com
An n×n square matrix A over a field, with n≥1, is singular when it has no matrix inverse. Geometrically, its linear map loses at least one input direction: some nonzero vector v satisfies Av=0, so A(x+v)=Ax. Over the real numbers, the following family makes that loss visible:
A(t)=(10​0t​),A(t)(x,y)=(x,ty).
(60)
For this diagonal matrix, detA(t)=t. Whenever t=0, the input can be recovered as (x,y)=(b1​,b2​/t) and the kernel is {0}. At t=0, the kernel becomes span{(0,1)}: the entire second coordinate is forgotten. Consequently A(0)x=(b1​,b2​) has no solution if b2​=0, and has the solution straight line x=(b1​,s), s∈R, if b2​=0. A singular matrix therefore need not make a particular linear system inconsistent; it prevents unique recovery when that linear system is consistent.
For an n×n square matrix, all these tests describe the same failure:
A singular⟺detA=0⟺rankA<n⟺kerA={0}⟺imA=Fn.​
(61)
Here F is the field of scalars. Equivalently, the columns are linearly dependent, the linear map is neither injective nor surjective, and some outputs cannot be reached. See the invertible matrix equivalences and Strang's MIT 18.06SC lecture summary, Multiplication and inverse matrices, p. 2. Over an infinite field, every consistent linear system for a singular matrix has infinitely many solutions; over a finite field with q elements and nullity d, it has exactly qd solutions. This follows by adding each kernel vector to one solution.
The square hypothesis is essential. For an m×n matrix, injectivity means matrix rank n (full column rank), whereas surjectivity means matrix rank m (full row rank). A rectangular matrix can satisfy one condition without the other; its kernel and image of a linear map give the useful tests without calling it a singular matrix.
Exact singularity also differs from sensitivity. For 0<∣t∣≤1, A(t) is an invertible matrix, but its smallest singular value is ∣t∣ and its condition number in Euclidean norm is 1/∣t∣. A change δb=(0,ε) changes the recovered input by δx=(0,ε/t): with t=1/100 and ε=1/1000, an output change of 0.001 causes an input change of 0.1. These are exact toy values, not measurements. The condition number quantifies this sensitivity before a direction is lost; see Steve Marschner, Condition numbers, §2. A small determinant alone is not a reliable sensitivity test: εI2​ has determinant ε2 yet condition number one for every nonzero real ε, since both singular values shrink equally.

Cokernel (cokerT=W/imT)

Words: 450 Articles: 1
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
The cokernel records output information that a linear map cannot produce. For T:V→W, it is the quotient vector space
cokerT=W/imT.
(63)
Its elements are cosets [b]=b+imT. Two vectors b,c∈W represent the same class exactly when b−c is in the image of a linear map. The zero class is the whole image of a linear map, so
T(x)=b is solvable⟺[b]=0 in cokerT.​
(64)
Changing b by an attainable output does not change its obstruction. This is useful because one can test compatibility before trying to find an input. The quotient vector space construction is described in Axler's §3E. [ref]
For the linear map T:R2→R2 given by T(x,y)=(x+2y,0), the image of a linear map is the horizontal line. All outputs (b1​,b2​) with the same second coordinate have the same cokernel class, because their difference is horizontal. Thus this cokernel is isomorphic to R via [(b1​,b2​)]↦b2​. In particular, (3,0) has zero class and is attainable, while (3,1) has nonzero class and is unattainable.
If W is finite-dimensional, the dimension rule for a quotient vector space gives
dimW=rankT+dimcokerT.
(65)
Compare this with the rank-nullity theorem, dimV=rankT+dimkerT. The kernel counts invisible inputs; the cokernel counts missing output directions. They need not have the same dimension: B(x,y,z)=(x+2y,0) has a two-dimensional kernel and a one-dimensional cokernel. A linear map is surjective exactly when its cokernel is zero.
The cokernel is a quotient, rather than a chosen perpendicular vector subspace. With a finite-dimensional inner product space as output, one may represent each class by its unique component in the orthogonal complement of the image of a linear map. That representation depends on the chosen inner product. For matrices over the complex numbers, this complement is kerA∗, leading to the cokernel compatibility equations.
The same quotient definition applies to a group homomorphism of abelian groups. For T:Z→Z given by T(n)=2n, the cokernel is Z/2Z. The equation 2n=b is solvable exactly when b is an even integer; the two cosets record integer parity. A quotient captures the obstruction here just as it captures a missing output coordinate for a linear map.

A rank-one matrix update changes a matrix A by an outer product uvT. For real vectors u,v∈Rn, its action on an input vector x is
(A+uvT)x=Ax+u(vTx).

The dot product vTx reads one scalar from the input, and the correction moves the output along u. All correction outputs therefore lie in one linear span. If either vector is zero, the update is zero; otherwise the correction is a rank-one matrix. The full updated matrix need not have rank one.
For example, choose
u=(12​),v=(3−1​),uvT=(36​−1−2​).

The update sends x=(x1​,x2​)T to the correction (3x1​−x2​)(1,2)T. Although all four entries change, there is only one direction of correction. Adding it to the identity matrix gives B=(46​−1−1​).
This special structure allows existing work to be reused. The matrix determinant lemma updates the determinant using one scalar, and the Sherman–Morrison formula updates the matrix inverse using an outer product. Such formulas are useful when a linear system changes slightly after a new observation or a parameter adjustment: the unchanged part can retain its LU decomposition. The term rank-one describes the rank of the correction, not the size of the entry changes. [ref].

Matrix determinant lemma (det(A+uvT)=det(A)(1+vTA−1u))

Words: 267
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
For an invertible matrix A∈Rn×n and real vectors u,v∈Rn, the matrix determinant lemma states
det(A+uvT)=det(A)(1+vTA−1u).
(69)
The expression vTA−1u is a scalar, so a rank-one matrix update changes the determinant by a single multiplicative factor. One need not expand the updated determinant entry by entry.
For the preceding example with A=I, the dot product is vTu=3−2=1. Hence the updated determinant is 1+1=2. Direct evaluation confirms
det(46​−1−1​)=4(−1)−(−1)6=2.
(70)
More generally, let B(t)=I+tuvT for a real scalar t. The same calculation gives detB(t)=1+t. The determinant is one at t=0, two at t=1, and zero at t=−1.
A compact proof explains the scalar reduction. Put w=A−1u and factor A+uvT=A(I+wvT). If w=0, choose a basis starting with w. In that basis, (I+wvT)w=(1+vTw)w, while every other basis vector changes only by a multiple of w. Its matrix is triangular with diagonal 1+vTw,1,…,1, giving the required determinant. If w=0, the correction vanishes. This uses multiplicativity of the determinant to restore the factor detA.
The denominator in the Sherman–Morrison formula is exactly this factor. The rank-one update singularity criterion therefore identifies when the updated matrix inverse ceases to exist. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava use both identities for the symmetric update A+vvT in Twice-Ramanujan Sparsifiers, section 2.3, Lemmas 2.1–2.2.

Permanent (mathematics, permA)

Words: 668 Articles: 3
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
The permanent of a matrix adds the products obtained by choosing one entry in each row and one in each column. For an n×n matrix A=(aij​) with entries in the real numbers or complex numbers,
permA=∑σ∈Sn​​∏i=1n​ai,σ(i)​.
(71)
Here each permutation σ chooses column σ(i) in row i, and the symmetric group Sn​ lists every such bijection. The formula resembles the Leibniz formula for determinants, but omits the sign of a permutation. For a two-by-two matrix,
perm(ac​bd​)=ad+bc,det(ac​bd​)=ad−bc.
(72)
The absence of alternating signs makes the permanent of a matrix particularly useful for counting allowed assignments.
For a zero-one matrix, let rows represent people, columns represent jobs, and aij​=1 mean that person i can do job j. This is the biadjacency matrix of a bipartite graph. A product in the permanent is one exactly when all the selected assignments are allowed; otherwise it is zero. Each surviving permutation assigns every person a different job, which is a perfect matching. Thus the permanent counts perfect matchings. This interpretation and the definition are given in Yufei Zhao, Probabilistic Methods in Combinatorics, §10.2, pp. 178–179.
For a fully enumerated example, take
A=​110​111​011​​.
(73)
Among the six permutations of three columns, exactly three give nonzero products: (1,2,3), (1,3,2) and (2,1,3). These tuples list the chosen column in each successive row. Each product is one, so permA=3. Their permutation signs are +1,−1,−1, giving detA=−1. The diagram displays all three allowed assignments.
A zero determinant need not mean that no assignment exists. The two-by-two all-ones matrix has permanent 2 and determinant 0: its two assignments cancel in the determinant. The nonzero determinant criterion for a perfect matching is sufficient for existence, but the converse fails for a fixed zero-one matrix.
For nonnegative entries, the permanent instead sums assignment weights, with each assignment weighted by the product of its selected entries. It is then a total weight rather than necessarily an integer count. With arbitrary entries in the real numbers or complex numbers, even the permanent can have cancellation; the counting interpretation specifically uses zero-one entries. The permanent as probability of distinct independent choices gives another useful nonnegative interpretation.
There are n! terms in the defining sum, linking direct evaluation to the factorial. For the all-ones n×n matrix, every term is one and the permanent is exactly n!; the identity matrix has permanent one. Finding one allowed assignment and counting all allowed assignments are different questions. Their relationship to computational complexity theory was studied in L. G. Valiant, The complexity of computing the permanent, Theoretical Computer Science 8(2), 189–201, 1979. The elementary sum is useful for small examples, while the existing dense permanent approximation describes a more specialized way of estimating large counts.

Permanent as probability of distinct independent choices (P(X1​,…,Xn​ all distinct)=permP)

Let X1​,…,Xn​ be independent random variables, each choosing a label from {1,…,n}. Put their probabilities in the matrix P=(pij​), where pij​=P(Xi​=j). Each row sums to one. All choices are distinct precisely when their ordered list is one of the permutations of the n labels. These are mutually exclusive events, and independence makes the probability of one list σ equal to ∏i​pi,σ(i)​. Adding the list probabilities gives the permanent of a matrix:
P(X1​,…,Xn​ all distinct)=permP.
(74)
In particular, this permanent lies between zero and one.
For a two-person example,
P=(3/41/5​1/44/5​).
(75)
The distinct outcomes (1,2) and (2,1) have probabilities 3/5 and 1/20. Therefore
permP=53​+201​=2013​=0.65.
(76)
The colliding outcomes (1,1) and (2,2) have probabilities 3/20 and 1/5, totaling 0.35. All four outcomes are shown below; their probabilities sum to one.
If every choice has the uniform distribution on a finite set of n labels, then pij​=1/n and the distinct-choice probability is n!/nn. For three choices and three labels it is 6/27=2/9. This counts a subset of all nn ordered outcomes, not independent pairwise collision events. Independence of the original choices is essential: without it, the individual rows of P do not determine the joint probabilities.

Matrix similarity (B=S−1AS)

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
Two square matrices A,B over the same field are similar if B=S−1AS for an invertible matrix S. They can describe one linear operator using two different ordered bases, with the same basis used for input and output in each description. Fix the convention x=Sy: x is the old coordinate vector, y the new coordinate vector, and the columns of S are the new basis vectors in old coordinates. This is the convention of the change-of-basis matrix.[ref]
For a concrete linear operator on the physical plane, let T double horizontal components and multiply vertical components by five. In the old standard basis E=(e1​,e2​), its matrix of a linear map is A=diag(2,5). Choose the new ordered basis F=(b1​,b2​) with b1​=e1​, b2​=e1​+e2​. Then
S=(10​11​),S−1=(10​−11​),B=S−1AS=(20​−35​).
(77)
The second column of B says T(b2​)=−3b1​+5b2​=2e1​+5e2​. Its off-diagonal entry records how the chosen basis vectors describe the output; the physical linear operator still stretches along the old horizontal and vertical directions.
Take the physical vector p=2e1​+e2​=b1​+b2​. Its two coordinate vectors, and the two descriptions of T(p), are
x=(21​),y=(11​),Ax=(45​),By=(−15​).
(78)
Reconstruction gives T(p)=4e1​+5e2​=−b1​+5b2​. The output coordinate vectors differ, but the endpoint in the physical plane is the same.
This is why matrix similarity is useful: a convenient basis can simplify calculations without changing the linear operator. A diagonalizable matrix can be replaced by a diagonal matrix, making repeated application a calculation with powers of its eigenvalues. In the example, A makes the two independent stretch factors visible, while B expresses the same action in directions chosen for another purpose. Matrix similarity invariants separate properties of the linear operator from features of its address system.

Matrix similarity invariants are quantities unchanged by replacing A with S−1AS. Important examples are the characteristic polynomial, trace, determinant, matrix rank, and eigenvalues with their algebraic multiplicities. The characteristic polynomial convention here is χA​(t)=det(tI−A), where I is the identity matrix.[ref]
The short determinant proof works over any field: because tI−B=S−1(tI−A)S, multiplicativity of the determinant gives
χB​(t)=det(S−1)det(tI−A)det(S)=χA​(t).
(79)
Thus its roots, the eigenvalues, retain their algebraic multiplicities in any field extension where the polynomial splits. Also detB=detA. The cyclic property of the trace gives tr(S−1AS)=tr(ASS−1)=trA; equivalently, the trace is determined by the coefficient of tn−1 in the characteristic polynomial for an n-by-n matrix.[ref]
For the two matrices in the opening example,
χA​(t)=χB​(t)=(t−2)(t−5)=t2−7t+10,trA=trB=7,detA=detB=10.
(80)
Their entries differ, yet these quantities agree. Agreement is a useful necessary test for matrix similarity; it is not sufficient in general, as same eigenvalues do not imply similarity illustrates.
The relation also preserves repeated application. Adjacent factors SS−1 cancel to give

Bk=(2k0​2k−5k5k​).

More generally q(B)=S−1q(A)S for every polynomial q, so the minimal polynomial is also unchanged. Multiplication by invertible matrices preserves matrix rank, giving another invariant without finding eigenvalues.

A similarity transformation replaces a square matrix by a similar matrix. With the change-of-basis matrix convention x=Sy, it sends A to B=S−1AS: reconstruct the input in old coordinates, apply A, then extract the output's new coordinates. These three operations explain the order of the factors.
The equivalent formula A↦SAS−1 uses S as the conversion from old to new coordinates, reversing the role assigned to S above. For the opening example's numerical S, this opposite conversion gives SAS−1=(20​35​). If the old basis is E, the new basis vectors in that convention are the columns of S−1, namely e1​ and −e1​+e2​. Both formulas are similarity transformations; the direction of the coordinate conversion decides which one describes a specified basis.
An especially useful form is the intertwining operator equation

It says that applying B before reconstruction by S gives the same physical output as reconstructing first and applying A. Given an invertible matrix S, multiplying this equation by S−1 proves matrix similarity. Without invertibility, the equation alone does not prove matrix similarity.

For an n-by-n square matrix A=(aij​) over a field, its matrix trace is the sum of its diagonal entries:

The diagonal entries have changed but their sum has not. This makes trace useful for extracting a feature of the underlying linear operator without finding a preferred basis.
Over the complex numbers, or over the real numbers after allowing complex eigenvalues, the trace equals their sum with algebraic multiplicity:

No diagonalizable matrix hypothesis is needed.[ref] To see why, use triangularization over an algebraically closed field: an upper triangular matrix similar to A has the eigenvalues on its diagonal, counted with algebraic multiplicity, because its characteristic polynomial is ∏i​(z−λi​). Similarity preserves trace, so summing that diagonal proves the formula.

The trace of a real matrix does not give that linear map's volume factor: that factor is the absolute value of its determinant. For example, 2I2​ has trace 4 and area factor 4, but 2I3​ has trace 6 and volume factor 8. Their occasional numerical agreement in two dimensions is a coincidence. The connection between trace and local volume change gives a geometric interpretation near the identity matrix, and describes the volume rate of a flow map generated by a linear system of differential equations.

A proof follows directly from multilinearity of the determinant. Each column of I+tA is ej​+tAej​. The constant term chooses all the standard basis columns and equals one. A term containing exactly one factor t replaces just column j by Aej​; expanding that vector in the standard basis leaves only its ej​ component, ajj​, because every other choice repeats a column. This coefficient has a direct visual meaning. At the point ej​, the linear map x↦Ax has component ajj​ along direction ej​. Summing them gives its fractional area or volume change; the off-diagonal entries initially change shape rather than contributing to this first-order total.

System of linear equations (Ax=b)

Words: 825 Articles: 9
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A system of linear equations imposes several linear equations on the same unknowns. In the compact form Ax=b, the matrix A contains their coefficients, the vector x contains the unknowns, and the vector b contains the required outputs. Over the real numbers, the following examples exhibit the three possible outcomes: one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solution.
For x+y=3 and x−y=1, adding the two linear equations gives 2x=4, hence x=2 and y=1. Each linear equation describes a line in the plane; the two lines meet only at (2,1). Substitution checks both requirements: 2+1=3 and 2−1=1. The two measurements together determine both unknowns.
Keeping only x+y=3 leaves a whole line of solutions:
(x,y)=(3−t,t)=(3,0)+t(−1,1),t∈R.
(100)
For instance, t=0,1,3 gives (3,0),(2,1),(0,3). The direction (−1,1) belongs to the kernel of the linear map (x,y)↦x+y: its two contributions cancel. Moving in that direction changes the unknowns without changing their measured sum. The solution line is an affine space, translated away from the origin.
For x+y=3 and 2x+2y=7, the second linear equation instead demands x+y=3.5. The parallel lines never meet. In the augmented matrix, subtracting twice the first row from the second is an elementary row operation that exposes the contradiction:
[12​12​37​]⟶[10​10​31​].
(101)
The last row says 0=1. A zero row of coefficients is harmless only when its appended entry is also zero.
The column viewpoint unifies these pictures. If aj​ are the columns of A, then Ax=∑j​xj​aj​: a linear combination of those columns. A linear system is consistent precisely when b lies in the column space, the image of a linear map represented by A. Once one solution x0​ is known, every solution is x0​+h with h∈kerA, since A(x0​+h)=b+0. Conversely, subtracting any two solutions gives an element of the kernel. Thus the kernel measures freedom, while the image of a linear map decides existence. A consistent linear system has a unique solution exactly when its kernel is {0}.[ref]
Counting linear equations alone does not tell us how much information is present. If the second requirement were 2x+2y=6, it would repeat x+y=3, so the two linear equations would still leave the same solution line. The matrix rank counts independent requirements. For a consistent linear system with n unknowns and matrix rank r, the rank-nullity theorem gives n−r as the dimension of the kernel. This is the number of independent directions in which a solution can move. In the single-measurement example, one measured combination leaves one direction of freedom; in the sum-and-difference example, neither unknown can change without changing an output.

Rotation matrix

Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A rotation matrix is an orthogonal matrix with determinant 1.
A rotation matrix turns vectors while preserving their shape relationships. For column coordinate vectors in an orthonormal basis, its defining conditions are
RTR=I,detR=1,
(108)
where RT is the transpose and I the identity matrix. In the usual Cartesian basis of the plane, an active counterclockwise planar rotation through an angle θ uses
Rθ​=(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​),v′=Rθ​v.
(109)
Here the vector moves and the basis stays fixed: Rπ/2​(1,0)T=(0,1)T. Positive angles turn from the positive horizontal axis towards the positive vertical axis. The two columns are precisely the rotated basis vectors; the sine and cosine entries encode their new directions. Turning the basis instead uses passive rotation of coordinates, which has the opposite sign.
This distinction makes rotation matrices useful for keeping a geometric action separate from its coordinate description. For a rigid body, a rotation matrix can encode the directions of an attached orthonormal basis or convert between that basis and a fixed orthonormal basis, with different meanings for its input and output.[ref]
The orthogonal matrix condition preserves every dot product:
(Ru)⋅(Rv)=(Ru)T(Rv)=uTRTRv=u⋅v.
(110)
Consequently Euclidean norms and angles between nonzero vectors are preserved, as is the Euclidean norm of the difference between any two endpoints. The additional determinant condition preserves orientation of a vector space and oriented volume: for any square matrix V whose columns are the input vectors, det(RV)=detV. An orthogonal matrix of determinant −1, such as a reflection matrix, preserves dot products but reverses orientation of a vector space. The matrix inverse is especially simple: R−1=RT.[ref]

A half-turn about a unit vector n has matrix 2nnT−I: it fixes n and reverses the perpendicular plane. For every real rotation R, the difference R−RT is anti-Hermitian; it is also Hermitian only in the zero case.

Rotational symmetry group of a regular icosahedron

Words: 89
Rotational symmetry OurBigBook.com
The orientation-preserving rotational symmetry group of a regular icosahedron has order sixty. Its conjugacy classes have sizes 1,15,20,12,12: identity; half-turns about opposite-edge axes; rotations through ±2π/3 about opposite-face axes; and rotations through ±2π/5 and ±4π/5 about opposite-vertex axes, respectively. Conjugation carries an axis to its rotated axis and preserves the rotation angle. The transitive group action on edges, faces and vertices gives the indicated classes, with reversal of the axis identifying the two signs. A normal subgroup must contain whole conjugacy classes; none of the proper nonidentity sums of these class sizes is a divisor of sixty. Thus this group is a simple group.

Rotational symmetry group of a regular dodecahedron (Rot(D)≅A5​)

Words: 179
Rotational symmetry OurBigBook.com
The rotations in three dimensions preserving a dodecahedron form a group of order 60. There are 24 nonidentity rotations about the six axes through opposite face centres, 20 about the ten axes through opposite vertices, and 15 half-turns about the fifteen axes through opposite edge midpoints. Its nonidentity conjugacy classes have sizes 12,12,20,15: the centralizer of a rotation of order five or three consists of rotations about its oriented axis and has order five or three, respectively, while all edge half-turns are conjugate. A normal subgroup is a union of whole conjugacy classes containing the identity. No proper nontrivial sum of these class sizes plus one divides 60, proving that it is a simple group. The centralizers of the fifteen involutions are five distinct Klein four-groups, each containing three involutions. Conjugation permutes these five subgroups nontrivially. The kernel is a normal subgroup, so simplicity makes this nontrivial action injective. Its sign map to a group of order two must be trivial, since simplicity would otherwise force an impossible injection of sixty elements into two. Thus its image lies in the alternating group A5​, and equality of orders makes the image all of A5​.

Let M=(ABT​BD​) be a real symmetric matrix with A a positive-definite matrix. Its quadratic form satisfies the completing the square identity
q(x,y)=xTAx+2xTBy+yTDy=(x+A−1By)TA(x+A−1By)+yT(D−BTA−1B)y.
(121)
For each fixed vector y, the unique minimizing vector is x=−A−1By, so the minimized value is yTSy. Also, M is a positive-definite matrix exactly when S is a positive-definite matrix, under the stated assumption on A.[ref]
An original scalar example is
q(x,y)=2x2+2xy+3y2=2(x+y/2)2+25​y2.
(122)
Here A=2, B=1, D=3, and the Schur complement is 5/2. Holding x=0 would give 3y2, but letting x relax to −y/2 reduces the quadratic form to (5/2)y2. At y=2 the respective values are 12 and 10. Eliminating a variable therefore changes the effective cost of the retained variable.
This interpretation supports quadratic optimization and the positive-definite symmetric matrix tests used in Cholesky decomposition. In a multivariate normal distribution, a covariance matrix also gives a conditional covariance through a Schur complement; the required probabilistic hypotheses are supplied by conditional multivariate normal distribution, rather than by the algebra alone.

An invertible block A therefore reduces the question of whether the full matrix is an invertible matrix to the smaller Schur complement; a singular S makes M a singular matrix.

Coefficient-dominated entrywise positivity

Words: 89
Schur product theorem OurBigBook.com
Let real power series f(t)=∑k≥0​fk​tk and g(t)=∑k≥0​gk​tk converge on [−1,1], with fk​≥∣gk​∣ for every index including zero. If X⪰0 has entries there, applying f within two diagonal blocks and g across them preserves positive semidefiniteness. Indeed the coefficient matrix Hk​ is a bipartite block-constant positive semidefinite matrix. Each Hk​∘X∘k is positive semidefinite by the Schur product theorem, and their sum converges to the transformed matrix. Closedness of the positive semidefinite cone completes the proof. Convergence at one gives ∑fk​<∞, so coefficient domination ensures absolute convergence of both series throughout the interval. Without the zero-index condition, f=−1, g=0 and X=0 give a counterexample.

The real orthogonal group is O(n)={R:RTR=I}. Its tangent space at the identity is the vector space of skew-symmetric matrices.

Finite subgroups of the plane orthogonal group

Words: 130
Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
A finite subgroup of O(2) is cyclic or dihedral. Its orientation-preserving part consists of rotations and is cyclic: choose the smallest positive rotation angle, divide any other angle by it with remainder, and use minimality to force zero remainder. The smallest angle is therefore 2π/n for some n. A trivial rotational subgroup is included by n=1.
If there is no orientation-reversing element, this is the whole group. Otherwise choose a reflection s. Every orientation-reversing element is rjs, where r generates the rotations; these form the second coset. Since srs=r−1, the group is a dihedral group of order 2n. Its involutions are all n reflections and, when n is even, the extra half-turn rn/2. Consequently it has n order-two cyclic subgroups for odd n, and n+1 for even n.

Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
The smooth Gram map F(A)=ATA takes real matrices to symmetric matrices. At an orthogonal A, its derivative sends AH/2 to any prescribed symmetric matrix H. The regular level set F−1(I) is therefore a smooth manifold of the displayed dimension.

Cartan–Dieudonné theorem

Words: 72
Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
Every orthogonal transformation of a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from two is a product of at most its dimension many hyperplane reflections. In the real positive-definite case, a reflection normal to gv−v sends gv to v whenever gv=v. Composing with that reflection fixes v and leaves an orthogonal transformation of v⊥, so induction proves the bound. Each reflection has determinant minus one, hence orientation-preserving transformations use an even number of reflections.

Words: 65
Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
For real orthogonal matrices in odd dimension d, multiplying by their determinant defines a group homomorphism from O(d) onto SO(d). Scalar factors commute, so π(AB)=π(A)π(B), while detπ(A)=(detA)d+1=1. The map fixes SO(d) and has kernel {I,−I}. Since −I is central and has determinant −1 in odd dimension, O(d)≅SO(d)×C2​. In even dimension the same expression does not map every orthogonal matrix into the special orthogonal group.

Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
In odd dimension, the map A↦(detA)A is a surjective group homomorphism from the orthogonal group to the special orthogonal group, with kernel of a group homomorphism {I,−I}. Scalar matrices commute, and det[(detA)A]=(detA)2m+2=1. Together with the determinant sign, it identifies O(2m+1) with the direct product of groups SO(2m+1)×C2​. In even dimension, scalar multiplication by detA does not repair the determinant, so this construction does not give the same splitting.

R(t)ER(t)T=cos(2t)E−sin(2t)F,R(t)FR(t)T=sin(2t)E+cos(2t)F.

Indeed JE=−F, EJ=F, JF=E, and FJ=−E, which give both identities by expansion. The angle in this two-dimensional space of matrices is twice the parameter in the orthogonal matrix. These formulas hold in any finite dimension where the hypotheses can be satisfied.

A=(cosθsinθ​sinθ−cosθ​).

The reflection fixes the line making angle θ/2 with the first coordinate axis and negates its perpendicular direction. This follows either from the two corresponding eigenvectors or by rotating diag(1,−1). A nonidentity element of order two in a faithful representation must be either the half-turn or a reflection; the identity matrix is excluded by faithfulness.

Three-dimensional improper orthogonal transformation

Words: 74
Improper orthogonal transformation OurBigBook.com
A real orthogonal matrix T of size three with detT=−1 has an eigenvector n of eigenvalue −1. Its orthogonal complement is invariant, and the restriction there is an orientation-preserving plane rotation. Thus T is a rotation about the axis Rn composed with a reflection across the plane perpendicular to n. Writing the plane angle as ϕ, trT=−1+2cosϕ. A pure plane reflection is the case ϕ=0; if det(T−I)=0, it cannot be a pure plane reflection.

Special orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
Every real orthogonal two-by-two matrix of determinant one has the unique form
R(z)=(ab​−ba​),z=a+ib,a2+b2=1.

Indeed the first column is a unit vector, the perpendicular second column has one of two signs, and positive determinant selects the displayed one. The map z↦R(z) from the circle group is bijective and satisfies R(zw)=R(z)R(w) by direct multiplication, proving a group isomorphism. Writing z=eiθ parametrizes these matrices as planar rotations, with the angle defined modulo 2π.

Special orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
For positive distinct diagonal entries c1​<⋯<cn​, the critical points of this function are diagonal sign matrices D=diag(ε1​,…,εn​) with ∏εi​=1. Criticality forces CX symmetric; its square is C2, so it commutes with the distinct-spectrum diagonal matrix C2 and is diagonal. In the skew coordinates aij​ its Hessian is −∑i<j​(ci​εi​+cj​εj​)aij2​. The sign of each parenthesis is that of εj​, giving Morse index ∑j:εj​=1​(j−1).

Low homotopy groups of special orthogonal groups (π1​SO(2)=Z,π1​SO(n)=Z/2 (n≥3))

Special orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
All the special orthogonal groups are connected, and their second homotopy groups vanish. The rotation circle gives SO(2)≅S1. Conjugation by unit quaternions gives the twofold universal cover S3→SO(3), so π1​SO(3)=Z/2 and π3​SO(3)=Z. The special orthogonal sphere fibration SO(n−1)→SO(n)→Sn−1 propagates the first two homotopy groups for n≥4. In dimension four its exact sequence has a zero map from the torsion group π4​S3=Z/2 to π3​SO(3)=Z, giving π3​SO(4)=Z2. For SO(1) all positive groups vanish, and π3​SO(2)=0.

The last-column map p(A)=Aes+1​ has fiber SO(s), included as diag(B,1). Local completion of a unit vector by the Gram-Schmidt process gives local fiber bundle charts. Consequently it has the homotopy lifting property and the long exact sequence of homotopy groups of a fibration.
Surjectivity of special orthogonal stabilization below the sphere dimension (πr​(SO(s))↠πr​(SO(s+1))(r<s))
Words: 78
Special orthogonal sphere fibration OurBigBook.com
Project a based map α:Sr→SO(s+1) to Ss. Since r<s, the resulting homotopy class vanishes. Lift a based null-homotopy by the special orthogonal sphere fibration. Its endpoint lies in the fiber SO(s). If the lift moves its base point, right-multiply at time t by the inverse of its base-point value, which lies in the fiber. This keeps the projected homotopy unchanged and makes the lift based. Thus α is based-homotopic to a map into SO(s), proving the asserted surjectivity.

For a real skew-symmetric matrix M, M2 is symmetric and xTM2x=−∥Mx∥2. On an eigenspace with eigenvalue −μ2<0, every unit vector u has unit partner v=Mu/μ, orthogonal to u, with Mu=μv and Mv=−μu. Its plane and its orthogonal complement are invariant under M. Repeating gives real orthogonal two-dimensional blocks (0μ​−μ0​) and a zero block. Thus every nonzero eigenvalue of M2 has even multiplicity, the zero multiplicity has the parity of n, and the number of distinct eigenvalues is at most n/2 for even n and (n+1)/2 for odd n. Distinct positive block parameters attain the bound, with one zero direction added when n is odd.
